new_statements.quote: The wordlists are written in the official spelling of the Indonesian language. The sounds are more or less identical with those of Indonesian. [...] Geminate consonants as in dilla, daddoba are to be pronounced twice as long as a single consonant. Stress is indicated by the symbol ʹ, as in kiklé, pobóilo, if the word does not stress the penultimate syllable. [Bacan row, pp.133-147: kepala, rambut, telinga, mata, hidung, sumo, leda, gigi, nganggo, jantung, hati, bangkurung, tiól, tangan, tulang, dara ... manúsia, nama, laki-laki, perempuán ... dua, tolu, ampat, lima, enám, pitu, dualapan, selapan, sepulu ... -- all other Bacan items unmarked]

new_statements.locator: p.132 (conventions, under 'VII. In the Bacan archipelago: 1. Bacan. Spoken in the village of Labuha on Bacan Island...'); Bacan data rows pp.133-147; fn.2 p.148
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (20 pp., = PL D-46 pp.129-148; text layer + all pages rendered at 110 dpi and viewed). (1) Quote: p.132 (PDF p.4) reads exactly 'VII. In the Bacan archipelago / 1. Bacan. Spoken in the village of Labuha on Bacan Island, and used as a lingua franca in the Bacan archipelago.[2]' followed by 'The wordlists are written in the official spelling of the Indonesian language. The sounds are more or less identical with those of Indonesian.... Geminate consonants as in dilla, daddoba are to be pronounced twice as long as a single consonant. Stress is indicated by the symbol ', as in kikle' [kiklé], pobo'ilo [pobóilo], if the word does not stress the penultimate syllable.' -- verbatim as…
new_statements.rule_in_words: By the compiler's convention an accent is written only on words whose stress is not penultimate; the c.109 Bacan forms are left unmarked (i.e. penultimate stress) except tiól 'belly', perempuán 'woman', enám 'six' (final stress; enám has a schwa penult) and manúsia 'person' (antepenultimate, as in Indonesian). Inference: regular penultimate word stress with a few final-stressed items, the familiar Malayic pattern. The Coolhaas 1922-25 Holle list (Stokhof 1980, PL D-28 pp.87-103) independently shows the same picture: almost all items unmarked, a few with an acute on the final vowel (pará, sararó).
new_statements.exceptions: Marked non-penultimate items in the Bacan row: tiól, perempuán, enám (final), manúsia (antepenult). No rule for them is stated; enám is the usual schwa-penult case.
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation forms elicited from a single Bacan speaker met in Wosi (fn.2: 'I have not been to Bacan'); transcription in Indonesian orthography by an anthropologist, not a phonological analysis. Word-level only; nothing on phrase prosody.
new_statements.identity_note: Teljeur's 'Bacan' list is the Malayic heritage language of Labuha (bahasa Bacan = baca1243), not North Moluccan/Ternate Malay (nort2828): its forms (tolu 'three', habua 'one', danga 'hear', nganggo 'neck', sumo 'mouth', yoyo 'dog') match the Coolhaas 1922-25 Holle list no. 239 'Bacan' (toloe, saboea, danga, nganggo) and differ from Ternate Malay. Teljeur's remark that it is 'used as a lingua franca in the Bacan archipelago' conflicts with Collins 2018 (the inter-ethnic language there is Ternate Malay; bahasa Bacan is known to c.5% of the island, c.2500 speakers, Labuha/Amasing area). Data from one speaker interviewed in Wosi (South Halmahera), 1978-80.

sources.citation: Collins, James T. 2018. Penelitian Bahasa di Maluku. Ambon: Kantor Bahasa Maluku, Kemdikbud. ISBN 978-602-52601-2-4 (Bacan section pp. 14-19).
sources.note: Nothing on Bacan phonology or stress; classification (Malayic, close to Brunei/Berau/Kutai Malay), speaker numbers, history; refers readers to Collins 1983c, 1995, 1996a for the linguistic evidence. The only 'tekanan' passages concern Luhu and Kaibobo (Seram).

sources.citation: Litamahuputty, Betty. 2012. Ternate Malay: grammar and texts. LOT dissertation series. Utrecht (archive.org item 311-ternate-malay, scanned text).
sources.note: Only says there are 'differences, for instance, in prosody and the use of particles between Bacan Malay and Ternate Malay' and distinguishes that colloquial Malay from bahasa Bacan (the Malayic language, = baca1243); no statement on bahasa Bacan stress.

sources.citation: Paauw, Scott H. 2008. The Malay contact varieties of eastern Indonesia: a typological comparison. PhD dissertation, SUNY Buffalo.
sources.note: Bacan Malay mentioned only as a distinct, older Malayic community on Bacan and Mandioli (pp. 46-47, citing Collins 1983b); excluded from the comparison; nothing on its stress.

sources.citation: Visser, L.E. (ed.) 1994. Halmahera and beyond: social science research in the Moluccas. Leiden: KITLV Press (archive.org item 'halmahera', scanned text).
sources.note: Nothing; cites Collins' finding that Bacan is a Malay dialect close to Borneo varieties.

sources.citation: Stokhof, W.A.L. (ed.), with L. Saleh-Bronkhorst. 1980. Holle lists: vocabularies in languages of Indonesia, Vol. 2: Sula and Bacan Islands, North Halmahera, South and East Halmahera. Pacific Linguistics D-28. Bacan list no. 239 (W.Ph. Coolhaas, 1922-25), pp. 87-103.
sources.note: No list-specific accent note for Bacan (section 1.2 absent); a handful of items carry an acute on the final vowel (e.g. 90 pará, 152 sararó) while the great majority are unmarked; elsewhere in the volume the Holle convention marks accent only when it is not on the penultimate (e.g. p.67, p.122).
